feedback.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=3-3{t}^{2},$ where $t⩾0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=2\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=2\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time whan the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
feedback.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 3-3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ 3(1-t)(1+t) & =0 \\ t & =\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t⩾0$, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=1\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(t) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3-3{t}^{2}) \\  & =-6t \\ {v}^{″}(1) & =-6(1) \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(1)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=1\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3-3{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =3t-{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(2)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3(2)-{2}^{3}+C & =2 \\ 6-8+C & =2\,⟹\,C=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=4+3t-{t}^{3}.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(1)=4+3(1)-{1}^{3}=6\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$
